chapter_theme: Songs at Pothiyamalai (பொதியமலை), Agastya's mountain: the poet asks not to be debased by the beds of wicked women, nor to wither, diseased and laughed at by kin, but to be called near, given a place among the great ascetics and given the vel and peacock; the praise names Murugan as the one who told the word Om when Siva danced.

630.reading: The poet describes women whose kohled eyes, like Kama's arrows, change the heart, who wear honeyed garlands, whose breasts move under their bands, who cheat bashful men, kiss and speak sweetly, and asks whether, with desire for the bed of these wicked women, body and life wearing out daily, he should become debased. The praise names the dance of the First One, with Durga beside him and Kali with trident beating time, and Murugan who told the sacred syllable so that it stood by the word, the vel that struck Sura's host, and the son at the mountain with vetchi and jasmine garlands and the hunter girl of rustic speech.
630.nuance: தாரம் is a name of the syllable Om; சொற்கு நிற்குமாறு தாரம் மொழிவோனே seems to make Murugan teach it to the dancing Siva, though the line's syntax is unsure. விச்சை கொச்சை மாது: Valli, whose speech is rustic. செப்பு வெற்பு, if it names the shrine, is Pothigai.

631.reading: The poet describes women who loosen their hair, stare, shake their girdles and breasts, flash their ear-leaves and bangles, smile and frighten with sidelong eyes, call anyone, give their mouth's water to drink and make a man cringe like a dog; then disease comes, he is half-dead, and mother, kin and clan laugh as his body wastes. He asks Murugan to mark him, call him near, set him among the great ascetics, give him the vel and peacock and make his mind know that the Veda speaks of one. The praise names the battle in which Murugan burned the sea and broke Sura's mountain, freed the gods from prison and made Indra rejoice, esteemed by his father and uncle, at Agastya's mountain.
631.nuance: மாதவர் கணத்தின் மேவென: the plea is for a place among the company of great ascetics, not only for the feet. வேதமும் ஒருத்தன் ஆமென சிந்தை கூராய்: the Vedas speak of one. நாயென முடக்கு, crouching like a dog, is the poet's harshest picture of himself under women.

links.note: Both picture the poet laughed at by his own: in 610 wife, town and kin mock him, in 631 mother, kin and clan laugh as disease wastes his body; both answer by asking to be drawn to the Lord.

source_issues: Song 630: two corrupt characters, in மார்பினு஡டு (line 3) and வானினு஡டு (line 13), both read as -ஊடு, 'through'.
